item.title: Jane Foster, Venom, And Jubilee Will Join Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls As Year 1 DLC
item.description:
A couple of months back, we learned that Phoenix Cyclops would be the first DLC fighter to join Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls. He was just the first character in the game's Year 1 DLC roadmap, however. This weekend, the next three characters were revealed. Jane Foster as Thor, Venom, and Jubilee are coming to the game over the next year, and Jane is coming this Winter. Check out the reveal trailer below.

Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls has an interesting roster, because in many cases, they opt to take a lesser-known alternative to a popular character. Black Panther is Shuri instead of T'Challa, Robbie Reyes is Ghost Rider instead of Johnny Blaze, and now they've opted for Jane Foster over the original Thor Odinson. The reveal doesn't show any gameplay, so we can probably expect a more in-depth character showcase as her launch approaches. Jane Foster Thor is scheduled to drop in "winter 2027," which likely means January or February of next year.

The trailer also reveals the game's other two Year 1 DLC fighters, though they're not presented in engine. Instead, they're drawn in comic artist Peach Momoko's signature watercolor style. Venom drops next spring, while Jubilee joins in the summer. Venom's release will also include a new stage: Klyntar, the alien home world of the symbiotes.

For more Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls, check out our review of the game, then watch the reveal for Phoenix Cyclops, who joins the fight on November 2.

item.title: The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – October 9, 2026
item.description:
We’re in the thick of the busy holiday review season, and there’s no shortage of new games trying to capture your attention. As you head into the weekend looking for your next gaming love affair, we’ve got an impressive variety of new titles to keep on your radar. 

And if you’re simply looking to catch up on what’s happening in gaming this week, we’ve got you covered on that as well. 

  • Phantom Blade Zero Preview – Potentially The Best Ladder Climbing In All Of Video Games
  • Paramount Is Making A Live-Action Cyberpunk 2077 Movie
  • Grand Theft Auto VI: Here Are All The Songs We Heard In Rockstar's In-Game Radio Preview
  • Muramasa: Revenant Blades Preview – The Best Way To Experience One Of Vanillaware's Best
  • Nintendo Switch Sports Resort Preview – A Return Visit To Wuhu Island
  • We Got A Deep-Dive On The Dungeons And Monsters Coming To D&D: World of Warcraft

Star Wars: Galactic Racer

Wesley LeBlanc

Star Wars: Galactic Racer launched this week and it is worth your time, regardless of your thoughts on Star Wars these days. It is absolutely a Star Wars game, with familiar locations, music motifs, and characters throughout, but the IP is honestly the least interesting part. It is a truly fantastic racing game, with a sense of speed and tension that will bring you back to the days of Burnout (and it makes sense, because much of the team over at developer Fuse Games worked on the Burnout series). Don’t let the roguelite campaign scare you; it works really well and moves at a brisk pace that keeps the experience from feeling repetitive. And within that campaign is a great story, better than most in the racing genre. Once you finish the campaign, there’s still plenty of game left for you. With a standard Arcade mode, miniature campaigns in the Scenario mode, and an expansive suite of multiplayer races and tournaments, you’ll likely have Star Wars: Galactic Racer on your hard drive long after you pick it up. 

Read or watch our full review. 

 

Echo Weaver

Matt Miller

If you’re like me, you’re always on the look for new gear- and ability-gated exploration games that recall the joy of early Metroid and Castlevania games. Echo Weaver offers a new twist on that idea, by keeping the exploration element, but making progression be tied to knowledge acquired over the course of play, rather than new equipment. It’s a clever twist that has me intrigued from the early hours I’ve played. 

Our reviewer, Kyle Hilliard, has already had a chance to experience the full game, and had this to say: “Echo Weaver’s unique approach to the Metroid structure is admirable, unique, and well executed. The sense of discovery is fantastic, and though I realistically probably won’t immediately play the game again, the idea that I could start with knowledge of basically all of the abilities to rip through the game at high speed is an enticing one.”

Check out his full review here. 

Gears of War: E-Day

Alex Van Aken

Gears of War: E-Day rewinds the clock to depict the events of Emergence Day, in which protagonists Marcus Fenix and Dominic Santiago first encounter the monstrous Locusts. The series has referenced E-Day since its first entry in 2006, so fans (including myself) are eager to witness its portrayal in The Coalition's new release. In his Gears of War: E-Day review, Game Informer executive editor Brian Shea praises the release for delivering "an astonishing collection of shootouts, supported by improved traversal and tactical abilities, masterfully arranged battlefields, stunning visuals, and a strong, diverse arsenal of weapons and equipment."

Read the full review here. 

Order of the Sinking Star

Matt Miller

Thekla’s new puzzle game is a massive project with hundreds of distinct puzzles that fit together into a larger narrative and puzzle framework. It’s an overwhelming, impressive collection of brainteasers created by integrating several distinct puzzle games into a larger, coherent whole. In my mind, I’ve come to think of it almost like the video game equivalent of a frame story. No matter how you look at it, Order of the Sinking Star is a puzzle game built for experienced, patient puzzle gamers, featuring complex logic challenges that will push any player to think outside the box.

Deadlock

Eric Van Allen

We've once again got a great reason to dip back into Valve's unreleased-but-popular MOBA-shooter Deadlock. The Cursed Apple got a major makeover with its latest update, and a new slate of heroes is looking to join the roster, with playtime counting toward votes on which character joins each week. We've already seen the Rat King and the sweet old Baba win the vote, but four more are still on the way. The graphics overhaul is huge, though; not only do the streets and boulevards of this cursed New York look phenomenal, but small UI and indicator tweaks have made Deadlock even easier to read at a glance. Deadlock remains the most impressive game not officially released, and if you can get an invite, it's worth diving in this weekend to see what the team has been cooking up.

The Old King’s Crown

Matt Miller

One of the most intriguing and tactically rich games of the last several years, The Old King’s Crown is a true triumph for integrating numerous mechanics into a thematically rich narrative framework. Each player takes on the role of a potential inheritor of the monarchy after the old king dies. Using bluffing, card management, and control of the game board, each player controls a faction that is subtly distinct from the others, leading to a fascinating emergent narrative, like a rebellious uprising seizing control from the old nobility. Unfortunately, the biggest challenge for your weekend enjoyment of the title might be tracking down a copy; Eerie Idol’s excellent game is so celebrated it can be hard to find a copy. But if you’re lucky enough to find a way to play, I think you’ll be happy to add it to your shelf. If you can’t, it was just one of the titles that won accolades in our list of the very best board games of 2025, and you could try to snag one of those instead.

item.title: Mafia III Gets Surprise PS5, Xbox Series X/S 60 FPS Update Today, And It's Free If You Already Own The Game
item.description:
2K Games has surprise-dropped a PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S update for Mafia III that adds 60 FPS performance to the game alongside other technical improvements. If you already own the game on PlayStation 4 or Xbox One, the update is free; if you don't, 2K is currently selling it on digital storefronts at 80% off. 

The publisher has also revealed Mafia III: Definitive Edition for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S as well, and it includes the base game, all story DLC (Faster, Baby!, Stones Unturned, and Sign of the Times), and bonus packs (Family Kick-Back Pack and the Judge, Jury, & Executioner Weapons Pack) bundled together. This definitive edition is also available in the recently released Mafia: The Omerta Collection, which features Mafia, Mafia II, Mafia III, and Mafia: The Old Country. 

Check out Mafia III in 60 FPS in the new trailer below: 

Alongside today's update, the Steam version of the game is getting a massive patch with all kinds of fixes, improvements, quality-of-life updates, and more. You can read those patch notes here. 

For more, read Game Informer's Mafia III review, and then check out our thoughts on last year's Mafia: The Old Country.

item.title: Forza Horizon 6 On PS5 Delayed To 2027, Will Launch Alongside Game's First Premium Expansion
item.description:
Forza Horizon 6, the latest open-world racer from developer Playground Games, was set to launch on PlayStation 5 this year but has since been delayed to 2027. Fortunately, it launches early in the year, specifically on January 26. 

If you pay for the more expensive Premium Edition of Forza Horizon 6, you can start the game five days early on January 21, which is the same day the game's first paid premium expansion goes live on all platforms (including PS5). A physical version of Forza Horizon 6 will be available on disc for PS5 at launch from retailers. Developer Panic Button, which is the studio behind the PS5 version of Forza Horizon 5 that launched last year, is behind this PS5 port of Forza Horizon 6. 

You can check out Forza Horizon 6 running on PlayStation 5's 4K/30 FPS Quality Mode in the trailer below: 

Playground Games says a 60 FPS Performance mode will also be available, though it hasn't shared details on how the game might run on PlayStation 5 Pro. 

If you preorder the game, you will get the pre-tuned Ferrari J50 added to your garage in-game after completing the prologue. 

Forza Horizon 6 on PS5 will support cross-platform and cross-save with the Xbox and Steam versions. Plus, the game's user-generated content is cross-platform, so PS5 players will have access to a large, growing collection of community-created content at launch. That content includes player-made EventLab races, Prefab vehicles, Garages, Estates, Liveries, and Tuning Setups. 

Forza Horizon 6 hits PS5 in early access on January 21, ahead of its full launch on January 26. 

In the meantime, read Game Informer's Forza Horizon 6 review. 

[Editor’s Note: This article previously incorrectly stated the premium expansion will be free. It will not be free.]

item.title: Paramount Is Making A Live-Action Cyberpunk 2077 Movie With The Producer Of Transformers One
item.description:
Paramount Pictures is making a live-action Cyberpunk 2077 movie, according to a Deadline report. The publication says the movie is set in the Cyberpunk 2077 universe, which began with CD Projekt Red's RPG of the same name and has since expanded into novels, comics, and anime like Cyberpunk: Edgerunners (which is getting a sequel this month). 

Transformers One producer Lorenzo di Bonaventure, who has also produced multiple Transformers films, Snake Eyes, Madame Web, and more, is producing this Cyberpunk 2077 live-action movie. Beyond that, little else is known. 

Cyberpunk 2077 is rich with stories, whether that's the main story about V and Johnny Silverhand and their attempt to bring down Arasaka Corporation, the spy-centric Phantom Liberty expansion, or any of its myriad side quests, so Paramount has plenty to draw on for this film. It sounds like this movie is still early in development, possibly even before pre-production, so it could be a while before we learn more. 

Notably, Paramount is also co-producing the upcoming Street Fighter movie hitting theaters next week, and it's working on a live-action movie based on Activision's long-running Call of Duty series, with Deepwater Horizon director Peter Berg on board to direct. 

In the meantime, read Game Informer's Cyberpunk 2077 review, and then read our review of the Phantom Liberty expansion. 

[Source: Deadline]

item.description:
Rockstar Games is gearing up for the long-awaited launch of Grand Theft Auto VI next month on November 19. We've been learning more about its protagonists, Jason and Lucia, the city of Leonida, and the in-game weather systems and wildlife players can expect to see. Now, Rockstar is letting players preview six radio stations in Grand Theft Auto VI. 

You can find these radio previews here, and each features snippets of the hosts and songs you can expect to hear; the previews run roughly 1 to 3 minutes long. Alongside these radios you can listen to in-game, Rockstar has revealed that Grand Theft Auto VI will feature a series of "on-demand podcasts, with both radio and podcasts available to listen to in vehicles or on foot through newly introduced headphones and earbuds connected to their smartphones." 

Below, we'll list each of the radio stations Rockstar has detailed today: 

Cocoteo FM

Leonida's home for the best of modern Latin music. Hosted by El Martillo and La Gata and featuring everything from bachata and merengue to dembow and reggaeton – Cocoteo FM is el party que nunca se apaga.

Back Country Radio

MW and Delta Dawne blast renegade country music to the Grassrivers, Port Gellhorn, and beyond. Stay tuned for Back Country’s roving reporter, swamp meteorologist, and Delta’s not-so-secret lover Mud Dog Mike checking in from the driver’s seat of his Grassrivers airboat.

AfroBank FM

Turn up the gbedu with Burna and Palmsy, AfroBank FM's dynamic duo curating the best in African music, from 20th-century classics and undiscovered gems to contemporary sounds like amapiano, 3-step, and more.

Crushing metal has landed in Leonida. Jump in the pit with DJ Kerry and DJ Tom for classic metal from the ‘80s and beyond as they channel Leonida’s deep metal roots.

Flash FM

The Vice City institution that delivers the best in pop music with Robyn and Alex — guaranteed to make you dance no matter where you find yourself in the Goodtime State.

Dirty South Classics

A little southern hospitality from Trick and Trina, blasting regional rap and hip-hop classics. From the beach to the block, nobody reps Leonida and the South like they do.

And that's a look at the radio stations you can preview today.

item.title: Exclusive Riftbound Radiance Reveal - Ziggs, Explosive
item.description:
It seems like just yesterday that Riftbound, the League of Legends card game, was bursting onto the scene with Origins. On October 23, its Radiance set will arrive with numerous new cards for deckbuilders to dig into, and today Game Informer is showcasing one of them: Ziggs, Explosive.

Long-time League players know Ziggs as the mid-lane artillerist and demolitions expert, flinging long-range explosives all around to maneuver, destroy, and cause general chaos and mayhem. Ziggs, Explosive makes good on both that vision of the League champion and his moniker, deploying special Bomb gear tokens on battlefields to tilt the scales in his player's favor.

 

Coming in at 4 Might and 4 cost under the purple "Chaos" color scheme, Ziggs can exhaust resources to deploy a Bomb gear token. The Bomb itself has a Deathknell: deal 2 to an enemy unit here, and kill all other Bombs you control here. Consequently, when Ziggs defends, he may kill a friendly gear to give himself an additional 2 Might this turn.

You can see the synergy, then: plant the Bomb, hold the battlefield. Setting Ziggs up with a Bomb on a battlefield means you can guarantee a pretty hefty swing in your favor when an opponent tries to take the field. Little combat effects like this fit the "Chaos" moniker, letting Ziggs keep a few variables up when opponents want to press in on his turf.

Additionally, we got a look at an alternative art for Ziggs, his BZZZiggs skin from League of Legends. My favorite part is the flavor text. If someone at Riot Games accurately assessed me as someone who enjoys a good Bee Movie joke, well, good job.

Riftbound's Radiance set officially goes live on October 23, 2026, with Pre-Rift events leading up to the release. If you want to keep up with all the card previews, head over to the Riftbound Radiance card gallery here.

item.title: The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – October 2, 2026
item.description:
Welcome to October, or as the world of video games and movies (and all other entertainment media, if we're being honest) refer to it: spooky season. It's getting a little chilly; a little overcast. And that means it's time to play video games where you count bullets. Or, alternatively, you fly a super fast jet airplane.

Before we get to our list of recommended weekend games, however, I want to share some of our most popular stories of the week. We officially unleashed our Grand Theft Auto VI cover story on the masses (subscribe here to get your copy in the mail very soon!), but I promise we offered more than just that this week.

But we are very proud of it and we hope you enjoy it.

  • Grand Theft Auto VI Features Tropical Storms And Hurricanes
  • Grand Theft Auto VI Includes Over 170 Animal Species
  • Star Wars: Galactic Racer Review – Very Fast, Very Dangerous, And Very Good
  • Stone Kite Is A New Studio From Halo, Destiny Creator Jason Jones And Author Margaret Stohl, And Its First Project Is About Rogue AI Robots
  • The Grand Theft Auto VI Digital Issue Is Now Live
  • Dune: Awakening Review – Only The Strong Survive
  • Gears Of War: E-Day Review In Progress

Ace Combat 8: Wings Of Theve

Eric Van Allen

Bandai's Aces team returns to the skies this weekend with Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, the latest entry in its arcade-oriented action-shooter series. Riding high on a tailwind of success from 7: Skies Unknown, Ace Combat 8 is a little bit more of everything: bigger battles, more intense dogfights, and a story that puts you right in the boots of a little-known pilot, thrust into a folk hero title as the new "Wings of Theve" after the current Wings is shot down. In the effort to take back your country from invading forces, you fly varied and dangerous missions alongside a charismatic crew. It's the drama that's really stuck with me, though. The Aces team is digging deep into ideas around the horrors of war, the losses inflicted and sacrifices made, and the intense aerial ballets you have with rival Shadow squadrons. This new Ace Combat is shaping up to be one of the better ones in the series, and anyone eager for some open air and azure skies should consider giving this entry a try.

End Of Abyss

Kyle Hilliard

End of Abyss is built by former Little Nightmare developers, and the lineage shows. The game has a mood that I would favorably compare to Little Nightmares (obviously), but also Playdead's Inside. Mechanically, however, the game is much closer to Metroid with a large alien (at least I think it's alien – it is intentionally unclear) map to explore and ability unlocks that let you get to new areas. You can check out some gameplay below.

 

I also spoke extensively with the developers back in May, which you can read here if you're a subscriber. Charles Harte's review should be online soon if it is not already, but I have been enjoying the game so far. The bosses have been more challenging than I expected and I have hit a few troublesome bugs, but it has been my go-to game to play in my leisure time, which is a big compliment considering how full my hard drive is with good games so far this year.

Minecraft Dungeons II

Kyle Hilliard

The original Minecraft Dungeons felt a bit like a family-friendly Diablo that blessedly featured local couch co-op – a rarity in the modern gaming age. The sequel keeps the train on the tracks offering more of what worked in that first game with iterative improvements. In their review, freelancer Tomas Franzese writes, "Minecraft Dungeons II proves this spin-off franchise can stand on its own and improve with subsequent entries at a time when Xbox is refocusing on its biggest IP. There’s plenty of room to expand, improve, and let me reach that endgame feeling of satisfaction much sooner, though. Right now, Minecraft Dungeons II is simply a straightforward, entry-level action-RPG." You can read Game Informer's full Minecraft Dungeons II review at the link.

Toem 2

Marcus Stewart

Toem’s laid-back but stimulating blend of puzzle-solving and photography charmed me in 2021, so I’ve been low-key excited for the sequel ever since. I’m a couple of chapters in, and while I’m not a great photographer in real life, I love a good puzzle game, and Toem 2 is hitting the right notes. Solving scavenger hunt-style tasks like finding missing lawn gnomes or spotting peculiar cloud shapes by snapping pics is easy and enjoyable. New camera tools allow more unconventional interactions, such as cutting objects by lining them up in a shot. Cutting down fruit from a tree to make jars of jam for a hungry bear or slicing pieces of fabric as a seamstress frantically tosses them mid-air is good, silly fun. I’m excited to see what other tools I unlock. As my list of tasks expands with every chat with the quirky characters, I get more excited to capture every photo op, find every secret and hidden path, and fill my book with more stamps indicating a job well done. After playing so many tonally mature, violent games recently, Toem 2 is the palate cleanser I desperately need and shouldn’t be overlooked if you like cozier puzzle experiences.

Fallen Tear: The Ascension

Matt Miller

This lovely new Metroidvania from CMD Studios is likely to surprise you with its breadth and size. It's a massive adventure characterized by a beautiful, vibrant visual style and an heroic story that is refreshingly free of pretension. While the game draws primarily on the classics of gear- and ability-gated advancement in the style of Metroid or Castlevania, its other chief inspiration is classic JRPGs. As such, the storytelling has an innocent, almost fairy-tale-like vibe, and you spend a lot of time recruiting new "Fated Bonds" that manifest as new party members that can step in during the action to lend a helping hand. Fallen Tear features gorgeous music and a surprisingly robust voiced script that carries the narrative forward. If these sorts of exploration games are your jam, you'd be remiss to not investigate if this one might be your next deep dive.

Blades & Battle

Matt Miller

Blades and Battles wears its inspirations on its sleeve. This is a pretty clear love letter to the medieval and fantasy hack 'n' slash brawlers of the late 80s and early 90s, like Golden Axe and Knights of the Round. Players choose to play as Arthur or Lancelot as they sword-slash their way through armies of enemy soldiers and monsters in local cooperative battles. The visuals are stylized and retro, and reminiscent of those early days of the genre. In line with its source material, the action is (likely intentionally) a bit stiff and unforgiving, but it's great fun to line up big combo juggles that send your foes bouncing around the screen.

This is the kind of game I especially like to surface in a weekend recommendation like this, as it's the perfect fit for a satisfying evening with a buddy, when you can't decide what else you're going to do with your game time. It may not have a ton of surprises, but it's a fun and satisfying time that nails precisely what it's aiming to do.

Heartworm

Kyle Hilliard

Heartworm released on Steam in July of last year to "very positive" reviews and this week it arrives on consoles. It's a Resident Evil-inspired survival horror throwback with 32-bit visuals and fixed camera angles. I have been playing it on PlayStation 5 and despite having just played Silent Hill: Townfall and being in the middle of End of Abyss (see above), I am enjoying it. Today is the second day of October, after all, so it is spooky season.

One standout mechanic I like is instead of the typical video game flashlight to light up dark areas, protagonist Sam uses the flash from her camera, which leaves a lingering brightness for a few seconds. The mechanic lends to the scariness well and also just feels different from typical survival horror games. If you're looking for something scary and nostalgic, take a look at Heartworm.

Ghost Of Yōtei Complete Edition

Kyle Hilliard

Ghost of Yōtei is one of 2025's best games and yesterday saw the release of the game's Complete Edition, which adds a single-player Echoes of Sekigahara DLC campaign and the new rogue comabt mode called Most Wanted (which features Ghost of Tsushima's Jin as a playable character). You can buy Complete Edition for $69.99 and it features the full original game and the Echoes of Sekigahara and Most Wanted expansions. If you already own the game, you can add the Echoes of Sekigahara and Most Wanted expansion for $14.99.

I have not had a chance to dive into these new modes yet, but am particularly eager to check out Echoes of Sekigahara. I am protagonist Atsu's biggest fan and very invested in her story so I will take more of that please. You can read Game Informer's Ghost of Yōtei review at the link.

Octopath Traveler 1 And 2 On Switch 2

Eric Van Allen

If you need more RPG hours than can fit into this weekend—literally—then Octopath will have enough for that, and many more weekends after. Both games are a love-letter to classic pixel-art, turn-based RPGs, where you hop between the stories of eight different travelers on their eight paths. Broadly, the HD-2D art is already a draw for the series, with absolutely gorgeous boss fights and locales throughout both journeys. The turn-based battles are tense, and building up your Travelers path over path is enjoyable. If you have to only pick one, play Octopath Traveler 2; the first game is good, but the second is easily one of my favorite RPGs Square Enix has produced in the last decade. Brilliant writing, an incredible score, and a very memorable cast of characters ensures you'll always have something to go back to when the weekend comes around.

Tabletop Pick – Cozy Stickerville

Matt Miller

The "cozy" phenomenon we've all seen in the video game world is certainly not isolated to that corner of gaming. If anything, the concept might even have a longer pedigree in the tabletop world, and we continue to see more success stories that tap into a low-stakes, relaxing, non-violent play loops. One of the best board game releases of 2026 so far fits squarely into this camp: Cozy Stickerville tasks you with growing a small town by placing stickers out onto the board. Players work together cooperatively over the course of multiple sessions to add new elements to the village. Alongside adding in farms, shops, and other important features, you're also managing events that form the story of the town as it plays out over years of in-game time.

You can't really lose Cozy Stickerville; it's more about seeing the story of your hamlet play out over time, resulting in one of several unique endings. But it's a lovely way to enjoy crafting an interactive story together with friends or family; the whole thing is low-stakes, easy to pick up and learn, and great fun to enjoy together.

For all of our recurring weekend recommendations, head here.

item.title: One Of The PS5 Pro's Exclusive Features Is Now Coming To PS5, Kind Of
item.description:
One of the big highlights of the PlayStation 5 Pro, now priced at $899.99, is PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR), which analyzes game images pixel by pixel and uses proprietary AI upscaling to deliver more detailed, stable gameplay, according to the company. Now, PlayStation is bringing that PS5 Pro-exclusive feature to base PS5 models, kind of. 

Revealed today, Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR), "a new performance tier of AI upscaling," is coming to PS5 starting today with Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei. PlayStation says QSSR is born out of Project Amethyst, its AI graphics collaboration with AMD, and uses a "streamlined neural network architecture" and "hand-tuned implementation that maximizes performance on PS5" to bring AI-guided upscaling to the console. PlayStation says PSSR on the PS5 Pro remains the "gold standard," but QSSR provides notable improvements in both image detail and stability on PS5. 

Two new videos – one for Marvel's Wolverine and one for Ghost of Yōtei – showcase the effects of QSSR, and while there's some improvement to see, it's not the most obvious... but you can be the judge for yourself: 

PlayStation says it will offer QSSR broadly to all PlayStation developers. It remains to be seen which games already released, or which games releasing in the future, will implement QSSR. 

In the meantime, read Game Informer's reviews of Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei. After that, read about the new Echoes of Sekihara expansion coming to Ghost of Yōtei, along with its complete edition, available starting today.

item.title: Reigns Developer Nerial Shuts Down After 13 Years
item.description:
Nerial, the developer of the Reigns series and other games, has announced plans to shut down. This marks the end of a 13-year run. The London-based studio posted a lengthy message on social media announcing it was entering “hibernation mode” after discussing plans to end active development with its publishing partners at Devolver Digital. 

“It’s been an incredible adventure. We came into this with no expectations or ambitions and we will never forget the utter puzzlement of releasing Reigns in 2016 to so many players, the fascinating and slightly disturbed Card Shark fan art players are still sending us, the thrill of Reigns expanding with adaptations of Game of Thrones, Animal Farm, Three Kingdoms, and the latest, Reigns: The Witcher. Not forgetting our most ambitious project, The Crush House, which we remain immensely proud of.”

Nerial does not provide specific reasons for the closure, but states that while the studio may be closing, the employees will remain working in game development following a break to “reflect on everything that’s happened before coming back with a new perspective.” 

You can read Nerial's full post below (click to enlarge):

Nerial burst onto the scene with Reigns in 2016, a card-based role-playing game where players assume the role of a monarch to rule and manage a kingdom. Reigns’ popularity spawned a series of sequels, such as Reigns: Her Majesty, and licensed spin-offs Reigns: Game of Thrones and Reigns: The Witcher (which launched this year and will be Nerial’s final release). Nerial also developed titles such as The Crush House and Card Shark.

Nerial’s demise is the latest in what’s unfortunately becoming a long list of developer closures in 2026. Meta shuttered three of its VR developers: Twisted Pixel (‘Splosion Man), Sanzaru Games (Asgard’s Wrath), and Armature Studio (ReCore). Other studios to close their doors this year include Bluepoint Games (Demon’s Souls remake), Ivy Road (Wanderstop), Intrepid Studios (Ashes of Creation), Spiders (Greedfall), Night School (Oxenfree), and Polyarc (Moss).

item.title: Stone Kite Is A New Studio From Halo, Destiny Creator Jason Jones And Author Margaret Stohl, And Its First Project Is About Rogue AI Robots
item.description:
Bungie co-founder Jason Jones, who helped create Halo and directed Destiny, has opened Stone Kite, a new Los Angeles-based studio alongside Beautiful Creatures author Margaret Stohl, who has also worked on film, TV, comics, and games (such as Destiny 2: The Edge of Fate). The studio's first project is called One Zero One and is set in a future where humanity faces rogue, AI-driven robotic soldiers. 

One Zero One kicks off with Part One of a four-part limited comic series of the same name, and you can read the first issue here. This comic speaks to the studio's aim to develop stories across all kinds of mediums, not just games. 

A cropped screenshot of the One Zero One Issue #1 cover

"Stone Kite was founded around a single premise: audiences no longer experience stories through a single dominant medium, and the creative process should reflect that reality," a press release reads. Stohl adds that Stone Kite is about breaking down old media silos. She writes, "Instead of starting in one medium and adapting outward, we bring the best global creators from different disciplines into the room from day one to shape the world together. We change the conversation. We never say that's how it's traditionally done. We build communities, and we listen to them. That's how we're creating worlds that people can explore for decades, in whatever ways they want." 

Issue #1 of One Zero One debuts today, and includes "never-before-seen excerpts from Jason's manuscript." New issues will be released through early 2027 and will grow with "prose, audio, and screen projects" to further expand the world of One Zero One throughout the year, the press release says. "I've spent my whole life making games, but I've always wanted to write," Jones writes in the press release. "I used to bike fifteen miles along Lake Michigan to the used bookstores in North Chicago, and bike home again with a backpack full of sci-fi paperbacks. Margie [Stohl] was the first person to believe I could write a book of my own, the first person to read it, and the one person I trusted to help me develop it into epic entertainment that leaves the world a better place." 

A piece of art from the Stone Kite website

One Zero One universe contributors include Eric Heisserer (screenwriter of Arrival, Bird Box, Shadow and Bone); Christina Strain (comic book writer and screenwriter of Shadow and Bone, The Magicians); Kris Anka (character and concept designer for Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse); and artists including Dan Panosian (Batman), Ramón Pérez (Hawkeye), Alitha Martinez (Wonder Woman), Raúl Allén (Dune: The Graphic Novel), and Hyeonjin Kim (Power Rangers).

Stone Kite's multimedia plan is ambitious, but not unheard of in games. Developer Reflector Entertainment intended the same for its Unknown 9 universe, but plans were put on pause after the first game, Unknown 9: Awakening, failed to meet expectations, leading to layoffs at the studio. Time will tell if Jones and Stohl's plans play out.

item.title: Kena: Scars Of Kosmora Delayed To 2027
item.description:
Kena: Scars of Kosmora was revealed in February as a direct sequel to 2021’s Kena: Bridge of Spirits. It was announced with a 2026 launch window, but as we entered a very packed autumn with no updates, that seemed less and less likely. Developer Ember Lab has now confirmed the game will be pushed into next year.

“Since our announcement trailer in February, we’ve been heads down bringing Kena: Scars of Kosmora to the finish line," Ember Lab writes in a PlayStation Blog post. "It’s been exciting to see all the anticipation and passion from fans. We can’t wait to share a new installment of Kena’s story with you!

"At the same time, we want to deliver a top-notch game that exceeds the quality we achieved with our 2021 debut, Bridge of Spirits, and at a much bigger scale. To do that, we need just a bit more time. Pushing our release into 2027 gives us the ability to really polish the expanded game experience we want to deliver.”

Ember Lab also elaborates on some of Scars of Kosmora’s known elements. The adventure is set some time after the events of Bridge of Spirits and sees an older Kena travel to the island of Kosmora. Kena seeks a cure for a mysterious affliction threatening her life,  but after her spirit guide staff is shattered, she must master Kosmora’s forgotten form of spirit guiding that lets her wield new alchemy-based elemental powers. She must not only cleanse herself, but rescue Kosmora from a corruption overtaking the land. 

“The ancient Spirit Guides of Kosmora developed their own unique approach involving the four elements and Alchemystic Temples,” says Ember Lab. “Four interconnected cultures once thrived across Kosmora, each with a guiding Element that fueled its society – before a mysterious cataclysm destroyed one of them.”

Ember Lab describes Kosmora as a large, multi-region map that “would take some time” to explore on foot. Thus, Kena has a giant wolf companion she can ride. “This ancient spirit not only serves as an exciting mount, but aids Kena in combat, both mounted and on foot, as well as solving Alchemystic puzzles,” says Ember Lab.

Kena: Scars of Kosmora is slated to launch for PlayStation 5 and PC sometime in 2027. Until then, be sure to read our review of Kena: Bridge of Spirits.

item.title: Xbox Disc-To-Digital Program Now Available For All Players
item.description:
Last month, Xbox announced a new disc-to-digital program that allows players to use physical game discs to access their digital counterparts. After rolling out this program to Xbox Insiders, it is now live for all Xbox owners.

Inserting an eligible Xbox Series X or Xbox One disc into a console will automatically grant players a digital license associated with that disc. In layman's terms, if you own a physical copy of Gears 5, for example, you will also unlock and download the digital version in your library. The original disc will still function normally afterward. 

The idea behind this program is to let players use their physical media to enjoy the perks of digital gaming, such as being able to access the game across multiple platforms and take advantage of Xbox’s Play Anywhere (letting them play an owned game across console and PC) and Cloud Gaming (which is getting hourly play time limits in November). 

Your discs just got a digital upgrade today! 💿

Now, all players can experience the benefits of digital with most XBOX Series X and XBOX One physical discs: https://t.co/TuUdSr7Or8 pic.twitter.com/IVgrV2NY4v

— — (@XBOX) September 29, 2026

A support page clarifies how digital licenses are tied to associated discs, stating, “A disc to digital license is associated with the qualifying game disc. Without possession of the qualifying disc, you may lose the disc to digital licensing benefits. For example, if you lose, sell, give away, or otherwise no longer possess a qualifying disc, access to associated disc to digital licenses may be limited or revoked.”

Xbox has previously touted its disc-to-digital program as an example of its commitment to game preservation, stating in August that “As technology, devices, and distribution continue to evolve, preserving access to the games people own matters more than ever.” This initiative comes as PlayStation continues to face backlash over its plans to cease production of physical game discs in 2028. 

In more recent Xbox news, the company laid off 268 more employees after cutting over 1,500 earlier this year, gutting Halo Studios and moving development of the next Halo game to Activision. The company also became the new publisher of Hideo Kojima's action-espionage game Physint after PlayStation dropped the project.

item.title: Suda51's Grasshopper Manufacture Is An Independent Studio Again After Splitting From NetEase
item.description:
China-based NetEase Games acquired Grasshopper Manufacture, the studio behind the No More Heroes series, Lollipop Chainsaw, and more, back in 2021. Now, months after the launch of Romeo is a Dead Man, the studio's latest release, Grasshopper Manufacture has split from NetEase to become an independent studio once more. 

Grasshopper Manufacture CEO Goichi Suda, better known as Suda51, published a press release today announcing the split, saying the decision came after thorough discussions with NetEase and "their generous cooperation." Romeo is a Dead Man is the only game Grasshopper released under NetEase.

"Having finally completed this all-hands project [Romeo is a Dead Man], as we reflected on the next stage of Grasshopper Manufacture's future, we found a strong desire to deliver titles in an even wider variety of styles to video game lovers everywhere," Suda51 writes in the press release. "As such, Grasshopper Manufacture has chosen to move forward as an independent developer once again.

"This decision was reached after thorough discussions with NetEase Games, and with their generous cooperation. We continue to cherish the amazing relationship our companies have built, and look forward to further collaboration when the opportunity arrives. Having improved our own self-publishing know-how, we now have a broad range of options available to us, and regardless of how our games may be published, we remain committed to creating unique titles featuring the 'NO GAME NO LIFE' gaming experience expected of Grasshopper Manufacture with our own signature flavor and further enhanced quality." 

This split comes roughly a year and a half after word arrived that NetEase was looking to divest itself of most of its overseas teams, as reported by Game File. In the past couple of years, that's been evident, too, with NetEase closing Canada-based developer Worlds Untold in 2024, just a year after the company unveiled the studio. In January, NetEase put Jar of Sparks, a studio it helped open in 2022, on ice; in 2025, it laid off workers at Liquid Swords, its Sweden-based studio it had invested in in 2022. Months after the launch of Marvel Rivals, a successful Overwatch-like shooter that uses Marvel heroes and villains as playable characters, NetEase laid off the entire U.S. team developing the game. 

Suda51 makes clear Grasshopper Manufacture is leaving of its own volition, with "generous cooperation" from NetEase, but it's possible the studio read the tea leaves and left voluntarily before being forced to lay off staff or shut down. 

There's no word on what Grasshopper Manufacture is up to now that it's newly independent, but Suda51 said back in February, around the launch of Romeo is a Dead Man, that the studio plans to release another game this year (thanks, GameSpot). That remains to be seen. 

In the meantime, read Game Informer's Romeo is a Dead Man review.

Naughty Dog celebrated The Last of Us series yesterday alongside fans as part of its usual September 28 "Outbreak Day." That's when studio head Neil Druckmann revealed that the team is working on two "projects" that will expand The Last of Us canon beyond Part I and Part II. It's also where Druckmann shared the studio's latest update on Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, its in-development sci-fi action game revealed during The Game Awards almost two years ago. 

Since that initial reveal, we've learned very little, though Druckmann has discussed the game's casting in interviews, and it sounds like we won't be seeing any more of it in 2026 either. In a Naughty Dog blog post made yesterday for Outbreak Day, Druckmann says the team needs to cook for just a little bit longer. 

"The team is heads down on what is shaping up to be Naughty Dog's most ambitious yet," Druckmann writes as a response to the Naughty Dog fan community wondering when Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet will be shown again. "There's an electricity around the studio right now as all the pieces come together, and we're stoked to finally unveil Intergalactic in all its glory. But... we need to cook for just a little bit longer. So we want to set expectations: we're going to be quiet for the rest of this year. In 2027, that changes. We'll fully reveal Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet and give you a proper look at Jordan's wild sci-fi adventure."

Druckmann closes by saying Naughty Dog knows it's been a long time since it's shared anything about the game, and it doesn't take continued support for granted. "We're working incredibly hard to make something worthy of your patience," he writes.

item.title: The Last Of Us: Naughty Dog Is Working On Two Projects That Will Expand The Canon Of The Series Beyond Part I And Part II
item.description:
Naughty Dog kicked off The Last of Us with the launch of the first game on PlayStation 3 way back in 2013. Since then, it has released a beloved DLC, Left Behind; a remaster of the PS3 release for PlayStation 4; The Last of Us Part II on PS4; a remake of the first game on PlayStation 5; and a remaster of its sequel on PS5. That's a lot of Last of Us from Naughty Dog, but it doesn't seem to be the end, as studio head and Last of Us co-creator Neil Druckmann has revealed that the team is working on two "projects" that will expand the series' canon beyond Part 1 and Part II. 

This news arrived yesterday as part of Naughty Dog's usual Outbreak Day celebration, which takes place every year on September 28, the same date the Cordyceps brain infection took over the world in the Last of Us games. While the day is meant more for fans to celebrate the series, Naughty Dog also uses it to tease what's happening at the studio, so it's no surprise Druckmann teased glimmers of more Last of Us. 

"Since Grounded II, we've talked about the possibility of telling more stories in the world of The Last of Us," Druckmann writes in a Naughty Dog blog post made yesterday. "We have a couple of very exciting new projects in very early stages – so we can't say much about them at this point. I will tell you that both projects will expand the canon of The Last of Us beyond Part I and Part II. The world of The Last of Us means a great deal to us, and we wouldn't return to it unless we had something meaningful to say. We believe these stories are worth telling." 

It's important to note, however, that Druckmann doesn't specifically say "games" – he writes "projects." While one would hope these are games, since that's what Naughty Dog is best at, it could indicate more of this world in the form of TV, movies, comics or books, or something else entirely. 

Considering Naughty Dog has yet to release Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, its upcoming action game revealed during The Game Awards 2024 almost two years ago, it will likely be a while before we see these additional Last of Us projects. In the meantime, read Game Informer's reviews of The Last of Us and The Last of Us Part II. You can also read about the latest casting for season 3 of HBO's The Last of Us, which includes John Goodman. After that, check out our list of the top 10 PlayStation 5 games.

item.title: The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – September 25, 2026
item.description:
Hey! I hope you're getting ready to have a good weekend or whatever, but did you see that we announced the next Game Informer cover? It's Grand Theft Auto VI, baby. We have a 14-page story with exclusive interviews with members of the Rockstar development team, brand new screenshots, and gorgeous original cover art. We're very, very excited about it. Subscribe now to make sure you get your copy of the issue in the mail!

The cover story? That will be available for subscribers to read digitally next week. And the actual Grand Theft Auto VI game? That releases November 19. That doesn't help you right now. Thankfully, we have weekend recommendations below that you can play right now. But before all that, here are some of the biggest stories of the week.

  • Cover Reveal – Grand Theft Auto VI 
  • Check Out The Design Document For Sonic Adventure 2's Iconic City Escape Level 
  • One Of Mouthwashing Publisher Critical Reflex's Demos Made Me Gag (Plus, Three Other Games I Can't Wait For) 
  • Final Fantasy VII Revelation Preview - Playing Chapter 1 Gave Me Exactly What I Was Looking For After A Disappointing And Overwhelming Gamescom Demo
  • StarCraft Devs Answer Our Biggest Questions at BlizzCon | Interview 
  • Control Resonant Review - Fun, Frustration, And Fin Again

Control Resonant

Marcus Stewart

I wrote in my review of this sequel to Control that I love the storytelling, characters, and world, but that the enjoyable combat suffers from way-too-tanky enemies. Thankfully, Remedy swiftly released a day-one patch addressing this very concern. Although I haven’t yet tested the game to see how much it remedies my biggest criticism, I feel even better about recommending Control Resonant. Fans of the first game will have plenty to love and more, as Resonant boasts the same alluring surrealism and fascinating lore as the original, only blown out and spread across a big city. Dylan Faden’s powers make traversing a distorted and visually impressive Manhattan like a superhero feel appropriately cool, and the action only gets deeper and more entertaining as the story progresses. Boasting a strong cast and several memorable moments, Dylan’s adventure is a worthy successor to his sister Jesse’s.

Silent Hill: Townfall

Kyle Hilliard

Silent Hill has been on an impressive streak (as long as you don't think too much about the bizarre 2024 streaming series, Silent Hill: Ascension, or the recent 2026 film, Return to Silent Hill), and Silent Hill: Townfall does not break the streak. Since deciding to go all back in on the franchise, Konami has been doing a good job of enlisting development partners that all seem to understand what makes the series work. Townfall is not without its shortcomings, which primarily lie in the unfair difficulty of its stealth and combat, but the mood is spot on. I also enjoyed the narrative, which is about corporate nihilism among other fascinating and emotional topics. It also features Terry O'Quinn (of Lost fame) in a prominent role, and he is an actor born to be in a Silent Hill game. You can read Game Informer's Silent Hill: Townfall review by following the link.

EA Sports FC 27

Brian Shea
If you're still buzzing from World Cup fever, EA Sports FC 27 is out now. Though this new version doesn't change up a ton from its predecessor, it does give you more control of the players on the pitch, requiring more strategy as you push toward the goal. Off the field, a new social playground called The Grounds funnels players toward the multiplayer features, while continued refinements to Ultimate Team and the Career modes offer more long-form options. You can read Game Informer's EA Sports FC 27 review by following the link.

Kingdom Rush 6: Genesis

Matt Miller

It's pretty rare that I'll step in to offer a full-throated endorsement for a mobile game, but Kingdom Rush is one of those consistently fun series that always manages to pull me in. The new (sixth!) installment just released this week, and its tower-defense formula remains as fun as ever. While the game will feel mostly familiar to returning fans, Ironhide Game Studio has gone to pains to add some new twists to this iteration, including additional replayability for each of the 18 stages through five unique victory paths for each. The game has a whimsical presentation that belies the high challenge that can define some of the later stages. If you want an approachable game on your mobile device for wherever you're headed this weekend, it's a sure bet. It's also on Steam if that's your preference!

Wardogs

Eric Van Allen

There's been a hunger in the FPS space writ large, I think; a desire for the days of server browsers, lively interactions, and team-based asymmetrical warfare. Wardogs, an Early Access game from Bulkhead currently dominating the Steam charts, ticks all of those boxes. It's easy enough to understand that Battlefield fans can hop in, but it still veers plenty hard into the military sim to have plenty of craftsmanship in your chosen niche. Be a supply driver or builder, constructing forward operating bases, or a helicopter pilot ferrying freshly respawned fighters to the field, or one of those grunts, keeping a body in the hot zone at all times; anything you do builds towards capturing and holding the zone, and accruing your account match-over-match cash in the process. Wardogs has become a nightly ritual for my group, and has been the closest I've felt to days of scrolling Battlefield 1942 servers in ages.

Twisted Tower

Wesley LeBlanc

Twisted Tower does not try to hide its BioShock inspiration. Instead, it embraces it, using what players know of BioShock to set expectations and surprise; after playing through its story in about 8 hours in just two sittings, I can now add "delight." It takes place in the 20th Century and stars a man trying to save his love. To do so, he must travel to the Twisted Tower amusement park, a mix of BioShock's Rapture and Walt Disney World, with the abandoned twistedness you'd expect from the former and the hokey thrills and theming you'd expect from the latter. Using first-person, mostly gun-focused combat and some unlockable toys that give you abilities like dash and grapple, you will traverse five themed levels as you make your way up the titular landmark. All the while, Mr. Twister goads and mocks you along the way, in a very Andrew Ryan-esque way. Of course, there are narrative twists, scares, lots of blood, and plenty of demented employees who haven't clocked out of their Twisted Tower shift yet, awaiting you in each, and it remains fun from start to finish. It can feel a bit rudimentary in how much it leans on its inspirations, but it's one of the best BioShock-likes I've played in a minute, and it's perfect for an exciting weekend gaming jaunt.

Shinobi: Art Of Vengeance

Brian Shea
Shinobi: Art of Vengeance was one of the best action games from last year, but the Switch version wasn't quite as amazing as the other platforms. Sega hopes to remedy that with this week’s Switch 2 edition. Whether you're acrobatically exploring, slicing through hordes of enemies, or taking on daunting boss fights, Shinobi: Art of Vengeance is one that no fan of 2D action games should miss. You can read Game Informer's Shinobi: Art of Vengeance review by following the link.

Tabletop Pick – A-Way

Matt Miller

This recent card game is packed inside a tiny box that belies a surprisingly rich (if brisk) tactical play experience. You are charting a route for your spaceship to get from point A to B, gradually laying out square cards that will let you cross the far reaches of space. However, certain routes are only one-way, and specific actions (including those played by your opponents) can rotate the cards and block a previously accessible path.

As much as you’re aiming to speed to your own finish, you’re looking for ways to block your opponents. That adds a mean streak of play interaction that will delight many, but frustrate others. But the short playthrough length lessens the sting of being messed with, making this an extremely fun filler game in between other larger experiences during your evening of play. (edited)

item.title: Check Out The Design Document For Sonic Adventure 2's Iconic City Escape Level
item.description:
Few video game openings make the impression City Escape does in Sonic Adventure 2. After jumping out of a helicopter, Sonic uses a piece of debris to snowboard down the city streets as the generational earworm, "Escape from the City" blasts. It was a defining moment for gamers, whether they were playing it on the original Dreamcast in 2001 or GameCube in 2002. It's also one of the best-designed levels in 3D Sonic history. Ahead of its appearance in Sega and iam8bit's 35 Years of Speed: The Sonic Art Exhibit this weekend in Los Angeles, we got ahold of the design document Sonic Team used to lay out just how this iconic level would eventually play out while Sonic Adventure 2 was still in development.

Originally codenamed Project GAIA 2, Sonic Adventure 2 had the unenviable task of following up the acclaimed Dreamcast launch title, Sonic Adventure. Not only was that a daunting task on its own, but Sega found itself in dire financial straits as the PlayStation 2 was decimating the Dreamcast in sales. Sega, on the brink of exiting the hardware business, dramatically downsized the development team behind Sonic Adventure 2 and relocated them to San Francisco, California, which heavily inspired the hilly urban design of the game's opening level. 

"Our team of 120 got pared down to 11, sent to America, and told to go make Sonic Adventure 2," Sonic Team creative officer and Sonic Adventure 2 director Takashi Iizuka told me in 2016. "Part of what we had to resolve was 'How are we going to make the same game with 11 people when we have less than a tenth of the staff on-board?' I was really tasked with trying to make the impossible possible."

Regardless of the challenges, Sonic Team, under Iizuka's leadership, was able to clear the hurdles and deliver one of the Dreamcast's most beloved games in just a year and a half of development time. According to several long-tenured members of Sonic Team, including Iizuka, art director Hiroshi Nishiyama, and sound director Jun Senoue, Sonic Adventure 2 was their favorite game they've worked on.

"It was a small development team so we were able to condense all the good elements from the previous game, and deliver a story and game that was satisfying to players everywhere," Iizuka told me in 2022. Nishiyama followed up with, "I had a lot of new ideas for the game because of all the new stimulus and experiences I got by living in America and was able to make a game with a lot of great moments together with the other members."

While Sonic Adventure 2 is often remembered primarily as the game that introduced the world to Shadow the Hedgehog and songs like "Live and Learn," City Escape is up there as one of the most iconic elements of the popular title. The design document showcases various elements of the Hero Side's opening mission, including the aforementioned snowboard sequence, plus the chase sequence involving the massive GUN truck. 

You can check out the City Escape design document from Sonic Adventure 2 below, and if you need a little accompanying music as you flip through the pages, we recommend hitting play on the "Escape from the City" YouTube video above.

 

If you're in the Los Angeles area the weekend of September 25, you'll be able to see this in person, alongside other historical pieces of art from the Sonic franchise through the 35 Years of Speed: The Sonic Art Exhibit showcase at ARK/8. Admission is free, but attendees should register through Eventbrite. For more on the art of Sonic the Hedgehog, including how Sonic Team's approach to making art has evolved over the last 35 years, check out our conversation with Kazuyuki Hoshino here.

item.title: One Of Mouthwashing Publisher Critical Reflex's Demos Made Me Gag (Plus, Three Other Games I Can't Wait For)
item.description:
Publisher Critical Reflex was founded six years ago and has since curated one of the most unique, strange, and interesting game catalogs. If I had to guess, the game that put Critical Reflex into your game publisher lexicon was probably 2024's Mouthwashing, which launched the same year the publisher released other indie hits like Buckshot Roulette and Arctic Eggs. During Tokyo Game Show last week, I spent a couple of hours at the Critical Reflex booth, which was themed like an underground neon-punk bunker, and it was there I played four games that I immediately added to my Steam wishlist (even though one of them was so grody that it made me gag).

Below, I'll be discussing my thoughts on the following four games after going hands-on with each for roughly 30 minutes: Tiny Chills – Not From Ear, Grobnopolis | Last Days, Sated, and Flawless Abbey. Enjoy!

Tiny Chills – Not From Ears

Tiny Chills – Not From Ear

I don't know if Tiny Chills – Not From Ear is my TGS game of the show, but it is certainly the only game I played there that made me gag... so that's something. Don't worry, though – that's not a turn-off for me. In fact, I can't wait for more. From developer Docktopus Games, Tiny Chills is a horror/freak game set in a small town where earthquakes don't stop, and neither do the human disappearances. Nobody knows what's going on, and it's freaking everybody out, but that doesn't stop you from getting in a fight at school and getting suspended. Stuck at home, you help your mom at her ear-cleaning clinic, using a variety of tools to dig through patients' horrendous, wax-filled canals to clean out gunk, bugs, monsters (???), and more. 

The world has an overall Coraline vibe: something is off about my parents and the way they treat me. And Tiny Chills' grainy, shadow-filled, dreary lo-fi look sets it apart from other games in the ear-cleaning genre. At your mom's decrepit and lonely clinic, patients bang on the door as if the world is ending (and it might be?) and they're desperate for one last ear-cleaning before it all goes up in smoke. The knocks on the doors scared me every time – it was seriously so loud. Patients explain that something is itchy or ringing in their ears, and in no time at all, you're looking through their canals from a first-person perspective, guiding tools to the eardrum. 

You can use a suction tool to suck up clumps of wax and a hook-like instrument to latch onto bigger pieces, which you must then carefully drag out of the ear. There are other tools, but ultimately, your job is to clean up the ears and get whatever is clogging them out, and it is always. so. dang. nasty. Between the actual act of cleaning these ears, the squelchy, moist noises that accompany it, and the overall sickening vibe of Tiny Chills' atmosphere, my tolerance for grodiness reached its threshold, and I couldn't help but gag. It's disgusting; it's awesome. 

Besides cleaning ears, you do some strange things in your house, like catching a pet crow that flies around and figuring out where your mom keeps disappearing to. Something/everything is off about this world, and I cannot wait to learn more about just what the heck is going on in Tiny Chills. In the meantime, I'm going to prepare my stomach for whatever else lurks in the ears of this game's patients.

Grobnopolis | Last Days 

Grobnopolis | Last Days

Grobnopolis | Last Days uses a word – Grobnopolis – that you will say out loud once and then say it out loud hundreds of times afterward because of how good it rolls off the tongue. After playing it for roughly 20 minutes, I think Grobnopolis is also a game you should keep on your radar if you're into atmospheric horror games that have you asking yourself, "Just what the hell is going on here?" 

Set in Huta-Grobno in the year 1983, you are an apartment caretaker who's just trying to do his job while the world outside becomes blurrier and blurrier with suffocating smoke, the result of something gone wrong in a mine somewhere in town. Inside my humble apartment, painted with drab browns and depressing greys, I interact with various objects to learn the lay of this oppressive land. I eventually reach a radio, and by scrolling through live stations, I hear strange opera music, workers mumbling as they piece together what's gone wrong, and broadcasts warning of impending danger, a Church cult, and more. This radio seems key to Grobnopolis's narrative, as I'm clearly listening to stations I shouldn't have access to and learning things I shouldn't know. 

I interact with other people who call this apartment block home, and while none of them are outright sinister, something is definitely up, and they all freak me out. If I were this caretaker, you wouldn't catch me leaving my apartment, but specific tasks, like finding cords and other objects in the hallways to connect up some equipment in my place, force me to. All the while, a large crack or hole in my kitchen keeps growing, whispering things I don't yet understand. 

"From the black veins of the old mines rises a thick, blood-red ichor the locals whisper of as 'Soup,'" the game's Steam description reads. "It climbs through foundations, stains stairwells, and pools in places that should not hold liquid. Some things should never be unearthed. Some things were meant to remain buried." 

As this mysterious "Soup" makes its way to more cracks and crevices in Huta-Grobno, the local Church gets involved, bussing certain civilians out of town and out of danger, while asserting its control to gain power in the decaying city. I genuinely have no idea where any of this is heading, but Grobnopolis has my attention, and I look forward to learning more about what's going on here. 

Sated

Sated

Of the four games I played during my Critical Reflex preview during TGS, I think Sated has the most potential to be the publisher's next hit. It mixes something the indie space loves – roguelites – with monstrous horror fused with a little food-inspo by way of Cooking Mama. This demo wasted no time, putting me in front of a giant mechanical shark who hopped out of the water to hand me his hand/fin-written order. He requests some strange but not surprising ingredients, and though I don't know exactly what each is, each has a symbol associated with it. 

I take that order to my nearby fridge, which acts like a slot machine with a lever I can pull for another random drop of ingredients, and grab what I need based on those symbols. Sated smartly neglects to detail exactly how much of each ingredient is needed, instead giving you an ambiguous bar that shows how much of this or that ingredient should make up the entire recipe. This keeps you on your toes, because to make the most satisfying meal, you need to guesstimate as close as possible to what the hungry monster requires. 

 

After feeding the monster, you're given a score indicating how much they liked or disliked the meal you prepared. After that, you head to your underground train's captain's seat, select your next destination on a typical roguelite map/chart, and see what monster awaits their next meal there. Unfortunately, at the next stop, I fail to make a decent meal for the monster and, as a result, become the meal. I'm eaten alive, and my run is over. The hooks are there, and I'm ready for my next run; now I just need to know when that next feeding run will happen.

Flawless Abbey

Flawless Abbey

Flawless Abbey is both a surrealist, dreamlike kaleidoscope of colors and adventure, and a moody and oppressive mystery, and I'm interested in both pieces of its puzzle. In Flawless Abbey, you are a dreamseeker who lives inside a purple-and-grey facility where you hook yourself up to strange pods that allow you to explore an obelisk known as a dream-tower. While that sounds fantastical, it's just another day on the job for you. I go from door to door, trying to find today's pod of choice, only for it to break down when I finally find the one I'm tasked with sitting in. I walk to the IT person/being of consciousness who clearly loves the company it works for and is able to reboot the pod in question. 

I make my way back there, plug in, and find myself aboard a mythical train soaring through the stars and swirling sky. Aboard this train, I solve typical environmental puzzles, like one that tasks me with opening a door using a special mechanism I can only understand after using a train ticket as a symbol key. Throughout Flawless Abbey, I answer questions by selecting dialogue choices that feel less like answers for this game's world and more like ways for the game to learn more about me, the player. It's odd and thought-provoking, even if I don't really know what's going on. Visually, though, I'm sold, and the painterly, patchwork-style art, coupled with a far-out score, has me intrigued enough to figure out exactly where this train is headed. 

 

The game's Steam page promises more, like corporate benefits and health insurance, a beast trying to tear down the dream-tower, a personal assistant who will guide me through dreams (even though they are also terrified about what's going on), and other dreamseekers to meet. "Something isn't right," the game's description reads, and I agree, but I'll have to wait for the game's launch to learn what's wrong.

item.title: Ace Attorney: Dual Destinies VR Was Just Announced For 2027 – I Have Some Objections
item.description:
Ace Attorney fans have been hoping for the announcement of a new entry for many years now, but today, we got a surprise instead. Ace Attorney: Dual Destinies VR is a virtual reality version of the fifth mainline game in Capcom's lawyer-themed adventure series, and it's coming to Meta platforms next year. You can watch the reveal trailer below.

This port gives Dual Destinies a more hands-on approach, allowing players to pick up evidence to inspect, examine environments for clues in first person, and use gestures and voice commands during cross-examinations: You can literally yell "Objection!" to object to a witness' contradiction. You don't physically inhabit the protagonist 100% of the time, however – dialogue during trials still involves seeing characters in third person, meaning you'll still get to see Apollo, Phoenix, and Athena's over-the-top animations. 

According to the game's store page, it will come to Meta Quest 3S, Meta Quest 3, Meta Quest Pro, Meta Quest 2, and Meta Quest, though developer Amata K.K.'s description of the game omits the original Meta Quest from that lineup. It drops sometime in 2027.

 

Personally, I find this to be an odd move for the series. Capcom has been generous and thorough with its HD collections of the older Ace Attorney titles. After the Ace Attorney Investigations Collection dropped in 2024, the only remaining Phoenix Wright adventure you couldn't play on modern platforms was his crossover with Professor Layton. As such, it seemed like the only next step was a brand new entry, so a VR adaptation is particularly surprising. 

Ace Attorney also isn't a series that needs to be a VR title. As fun as it might be to yell "Objection" every couple of minutes during a cross-examination, the vast majority of gameplay is non-voiced dialogue. Unlike the highest quality VR games, which work best in short bursts, Ace Attorney games are long, and wearing a headset just to mostly read text for a few hours doesn't sound appealing. 

Finally, Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney – Dual Destinies is my least favorite Ace Attorney game, but I understand why it was their pick here. It's the series' fifth entry, but it was the first foray into 3D, so it's the earliest release that could be reasonably set in VR. You can play it without playing prior titles, but I'd always recommend the original trilogy's HD collection over this one.

The best game to get the VR adaptation would have been The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles, as it's a better standalone adventure and it's been longer since that game's release (2021) compared to the HD re-release of Dual Destinies, which dropped in 2024's Apollo Justice: Ace Attorney Trilogy. But even though The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is a better game, Dual Destinies is shorter and has more of the series' iconic characters, so it's a more reasonable first project.

The silver lining is that Capcom is neither developing nor publishing this game (that's all being done by Amata K.K.), so there's a decent chance Ace Attorney 7 is still in the works – the development team won't be preoccupied with finishing this VR title first. Maybe this VR version will drastically change my opinion of Dual Destinies, but it's unlikely. I'll find out when the game drops sometime next year.

item.title: Control Resonant Launch Patch Will Address Its Biggest Combat Complaints
item.description:
Control Resonant launches today, and the game’s first update will address one of its biggest pre-release criticisms: its enemies take too long to defeat, and protagonist Dylan Faden feels too weak. While early access players and reviewers, including us, had to endure a much harder game in the weeks before release, the wider player base will likely have a smoother ride thanks to this hotfix.

Developer Remedy Entertainment has announced in a blog post that after reading reviews (which have overall been very positive despite the combat critiques), and early player impressions, “we have decided to deploy a hotfix (1.3.3) at launch to address a few specific things: enemy health pools feeling too high, requiring too many hits to Falter (stun) enemies for executions, and Dylan’s overall combat strength early on in the game not feeling powerful enough (even if the man just woke up from a coma).”

To improve the combat flow and overall experience, the launch update will do the following:

  • Reduce the base health and required Falter (stun) level of most enemies, as well as the Dancer and Deserter bosses
  • Increase maximum Aberrant Strength and maximum Ability Strength
  • These strength increases follow a curve, with progressively larger increases towards the end. The more upgrades you have, the more damage you deal.

The patch will also lower the cost of respeccing the ability tree, and vendors will also carry more stock of the special resource required to respec. A UI text update aims to better explain Build Power and Aberrant (Dylan’s primary weapon) strength. This will take the following forms;

  • Aberrant Strength: “Multiplier X%” will now be: “Damage and Falter X%”.
  • Build Power: “Calculated based on equipped Weapon Forms, Talents and Core Upgrades.” will now be: “From unlocked Combat Abilities, Aberrant forms/upgrades, Talents, and Core Upgrades.”

Remedy promises to continue working on other known issues in Control Resonant as players begin diving into the sequel today. Overall, despite some combat headaches, we enjoyed Control Resonant quite a bit, scoring it an 8.5 out of 10. Be sure to read our full review.

item.title: Iizuka: Working With Sonic Mania Devs Again 'Not Off The Books Yet,' 'There's Definitely A Desire'
item.description:
The release of Sonic Mania in 2017 signaled to many fans that Sega and the Sonic the Hedgehog franchise were listening to fans. Announced as part of the series' 25th anniversary in 2016, the title was developed as a collaboration between Sonic Team and a group of independent developers led by designer Christian Whitehead. Following the release and subsequent overwhelming acclaim of Sonic Mania and its upgraded version, Sonic Mania Plus, Sonic Team entered into conversations with Evening Star, the studio founded by Whitehead and several other members of the Sonic Mania dev team in 2018, but despite getting into the prototyping phase, that sequel never happened. 

In 2023, a Sonic Mania sequel felt like a distant hope, as Evening Star announced its own platformer, Penny's Big Breakaway, while Sega released its next 2D Sonic game, Sonic Superstars, which was developed in collaboration with Sonic co-creator Naoto Ohshima's studio, Arzest. When I broached the Sonic Mania 2 topic with Iizuka a few years ago, he confirmed that those initial conversations occurred with Evening Star. "There was a period after the development of Sonic Mania when we worked with them to consider concepts for the next generation of Classic Sonic," Iizuka said in 2023. "It's too bad that it didn't become a finished game. Still, I'm pleased that the next generation of Classic Sonic that we talked about with them has been achieved with Superstars."

Sonic Superstars

Iizuka mentions that he wanted to go a different route with Mania's successor, instead relying on 3D models instead of pixel-art graphics to appeal to a wider audience. Whitehead, for his part, backed up Iizuka's retelling of the events. "When we started Evening Star, it was always our goal to move beyond 2D pixel art into 3D games, and develop all-new, original IP," he says. "Evening Star did work with Sega to explore possible directions Classic Sonic could go after the success of Sonic Mania. Sonic Mania 2 was never in development, though, because we actually agreed early on that we should try to make something fresh, like hand-drawn 2D or 2.5D. At the same time, Evening Star was developing our new Star Engine, so we also ended up making a cool Sonic prototype that played with depth in 2.5D, and some other gameplay ideas. As Iizuka-san said, though, [Evening Star] did not continue to full production on the game, at which point Arzest took the helm and made Superstars alongside Sonic Team. We moved forward with our plans to develop an original 3D title, which is, of course, Penny's Big Breakaway!"

Now, three years following that conversation, Sonic Team is collaborating with TecoPark for Sonic Pico Park, releasing this November. When I ask Iizuka what he looks for when selecting a development partner, he says studios and developers that can fill gaps where Sonic Team isn't as skilled or experienced are an important factor. "Sonic Team is really proficient at making action games; they make action game after action game," Iizuka says. "The Pico Park team, they’re really good at making that action-puzzle format. That's something Sonic Team has never made before, so I wouldn’t want to say, 'Hey, Sonic Team! Go make an action-puzzle game.' But the Pico Park team, they're really good at doing it."

Sonic Mania

With Sonic Mania perhaps the strongest example of a project Sonic Team worked on collaboratively, it was natural to steer the conversation toward an update on the potential of Sonic Mania 2. While it isn't planned at the moment, Iizuka doesn't think the door is completely shut. "We're still really close with them," he says. "We've gone out eating and drinking with them because relationships are important to us. They also have a lot of projects that they're working on for what they want to do and what their business needs are. We don't have anything to talk about now, but there's definitely a desire to want to work with them again, and we think they could make a great game. It's not off the books yet, but it's not something that's moving forward currently."

I reached out to Evening Star chief technology officer Hunter Bridges to ask his reaction to the quote. To my surprise, he had already seen the quote from Iizuka when he read it in the latest issue of Game Informer. After reading it, he emailed Iizuka with the subject line "Eating and Drinking" (referring to his quote) to try to set up some time to do just that while Iizuka was in town for Tokyo Game Show 2026. Unfortunately, the timing didn't work out for Bridges and Iizuka to meet up in Tokyo this month.

"It's as he says, though, we have a good relationship with Sega and keep in touch," Bridges tells me. "We are working on something exciting right now, but it's not Sonic this time. But if the right opportunity lines up on both sides, we'd be happy to make another great Sonic game. Whether that would be Mania 2 is up for debate; we are an ambitious team!" 

Sonic Mania released in 2017 to widespread critical acclaim, earning an 86 on reviews aggregator Metacritic, including an 8.5 from Game Informer. Neither Sonic Superstars nor Penny's Big Breakaway reached the same level of acclaim, earning a 73 and 74, respectively, including a 7.5 for Superstars and a 7 for Penny's Big Breakaway from Game Informer. Neither Sonic Team nor Evening Star has publicly announced their next project, though Iizuka recently told 4Gamer that he wants to continue evolving both the 2D and 3D sides of Sonic.
